background.definition: Diphtheria is an acute infectious disease of the nasopharynx and skin. It is a toxin-mediated disease most commonly affecting the respiratory tract. The nontoxigenic strains tend to cause cutaneous diseases, which is usually mild.

list.listitem: Diphtheria is endemic in many parts of the world, including the Caribbean and Latin America. It most often occurs during fall and winter. However, summer outbreaks have also occurred.

Worldwide, 90% of all reported cases of diphtheria between 1990 and 1995 occurred in the non-independent states of the former Soviet Union. This was the largest outbreak of diphtheria in the developed world.
In the United States, the last outbreak was reported between 1972 and 1982, and since then, there have been only a handful of cases reported annually.
Diphtheria is caused by the toxin-producing strain of Corynebacterium diphtheriae. It is primarily a respiratory tract infection, but may also involve the skin or mucous membranes.
See table for risk factors.

Corynebacterium diphtheriae is an unencapsulated, nonsporulating, nonmotile gram-positive bacillus. Its virulence lies in its ability to produce a polypeptide exotoxin that inhibits protein synthesis. This toxin hence causes systemic toxicity, local tissue necrosis, myocarditis, and polyneuropathy.
In the first few days of respiratory infection, epithelial cells, fibrin, necrotic tissue, RBC, and WBC collect on the tonsils or pharynx to form gray-brown adherent pseudomembrane.
One of the early local effects is paralysis of the palate and hypopharynx.
Thrombocytopenia, necrosis of the kidney tubules, cardiomyopathy, and demyelination of nerves can occur as a result of toxin absorption.
The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) has recommended the use of DTaP as a five-dose series, including a one-time booster dose of Tdap between ages 11 and 18 years. A

Household contacts should be traced. Regardless of immunization status, close contacts should have C-diphtheria culture, be monitored for evidence of disease for 7 days, and receive antimicrobial prophylaxis. C

ACIP recommends immunization with the diphtheria, tetanus, and DTaP at 2 months, 4 months, 6 months, 15 to 18 months, and 4 to 6 years. ACIP also recommends a one-time booster dose of Tdap between ages 11 and 12 years.
ACIP recommends that pregnant women who have never received Tdap should be vaccinated in the immediate postpartum period before discharge.

Use of dexamethasone in preterm infants for chronic lung disease has been associated with reduced antibody immune response to diphtheria, pertussis, and tetanus vaccine. However, there is no demonstrable clinical significance in terms of increased rates of infection.
Localized pain at injection site or adverse reaction is not reduced by warming the DT vaccine or rubbing it in the hands.

Household contacts should be traced. Regardless of immunization status, close contacts should have C-diphtheria culture, be monitored for evidence of disease for 7 days, and receive antimicrobial prophylaxis.

Choices for prophylaxis are erythromycin 40 to 50 mg/kg/d for 7 days or a single IM penicillin injection (600,000 U for children weighing <30 kg or 1.2 million U for >30 kg or adults). The latter is preferred for contacts in whom compliance with therapy is questionable.
Proven carriers should have repeat pharyngeal cultures 2 weeks after treatment completion.

Asymptomatic close contacts who have been previously immunized should receive a booster dose if none has been given in last 5 years. Asymptomatic close contacts who are partially immunized/unimmunized/unknown immunization status should be actively immunized with DTaP, DT, and Td depending on age.
Patients who recover from acute illness should be vaccinated to ensure adequate protective titers.
Suspect diphtheria in patients with severe sore throat, difficulty swallowing, and low-grade fever. C
If diphtheria is clinically suspected, take swabs of the nasopharynx and culture on special tellurite media. C
Order toxigenic testing using the Elek test to isolate diphtheria toxin. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Markedly red pharynx with moderate to large amount of exudates and also petechiae
Painful creamy white curd-like patches in oral mucosa; easily rubbed off
Combination of fever, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly
Common cold prodrome such as nasal congestion and sneezing preceding sore throat
Gingival bleeding, with characteristic pain and dental ulceration
Associated preclinical sequelae; nontoxigenic strains linked to a case of endocarditis in Poland in January 2004

list.listitem: The respiratory tract is most commonly affected, but diphtheria may involve any mucous membrane or skin. Patients typically present with severe pharyngitis associated with pharyngeal pseudomembrane and extensive exudates. They may have respiratory compromise with difficulty swallowing due to tonsillitis and laryngitis. There may also be evidence of systemic involvement, including myocarditis, neuropathy, and generalized weakness.
The severity of the illness depends on immunization status either partial or total, site of infection, dissemination of toxin, and timing of antitoxin administration.
Early-onset sore throat usually occurs within 2 days of exposure. This can become persistent with associated difficulty swallowing.
Systemic symptoms such as low-grade fever, chills, headaches, malaise, and generalized weakness may develop by day 4.
Unilateral or bilateral paralysis of the palate may cause difficulty swallowing and voice changes. This may also lead to foul breadth and eventual respiratory decompensation.
Marked edema of the submandibular and paratracheal regions presents a bull-neck-like appearance. Associated epiglottal enlargement may lead to an initial diagnosis of acute epiglottitis.

Respiratory diphtheria is characterized gray or white membrane that is firmly adherent to the pharynx, soft palate, or tonsil. Nasal infection usually presents with initial serous then subsequent serosanguineous drainage, which is usually mild but often chronic.

Cutaneous diphtheria is characterized by a superficial nonhealing punched-out ulcer with a grayish brown membrane and necrotic sloughing. It is more common among inner-city dwellers and patients alcoholism.
Nontoxigenic strains of diphtheria have been isolated in patients with chronic skin diseases in Africa.

Systemic spread is usually caused by the toxigenic strain. However, there have been documented cases of nontoxigenic diphtheria causing invasive disease such as septicemia and endocarditis. This is more common among IV drug users, and the pharyngeal membrane tends to be spared.

Neurologic manifestation of the illness such as dysphagia, nasal dysarthria, facial and tongue numbness, is most often associated with toxigenic diphtheria. Other neurologic symptoms are ciliary paralysis causing blurred vision.
Myocarditis associated with dysrhythmia and dilated cardiomyopathy are also common complications of toxigenic diphtheria.
Nasopharyngeal and pharyngeal swabs should be taken if the disease is clinically suspected. Skin lesions should also be cultured. All isolated diphtheria bacilli must be tested for toxin.

Testing for diphtheria toxin antibody level before antitoxin administration helps make a diagnosis as well as assist in determining the prognosis of illness. Diphtheria antitoxin is then administered. Low antibody levels do not exclude diphtheria, but high levels signify likelihood of serious illness.

Diphtheria isolation requires special tellurite culture medium. Other media such as Loffler, Hoyle, Mueller, and Tinsdale may also be used. Once Corynebacterium diphtheria isolate has been made, the bacterial biotype should be determined. These are gravis, mitis, or intermedius.

Perform toxigenic testing using the Elek test. Information regarding the laboratories proficient in performing this test is available on the CDC website at https://www.cdc.gov/vaccines/vpd/diphtheria/index.html.

PCR assays done by the CDC lab help detect the diphtheria toxin gene (TOX). PCR assay is especially useful in patients who have already received antibiotics. It can provide additional supportive evidence for the diagnosis of diphtheria. Because of limited data, PCR is not yet a criterion for laboratory confirmation.
Suspect diphtheria in patients with severe sore throat, especially with difficulty swallowing and pseudomembranous pharyngitis.
Initial diagnostic testing should include swab of the nasopharynx and pharynx for culture, diphtheria toxin antibody level, and toxigenic testing using the Elek test.
Treatment with antitoxin should be initiated when the diagnosis is suspected, before confirmatory test results are available.
Dose for mild disease is 20,000 to 40,000 units of antitoxin; for moderate disease, 40,000 to 60,000 units of antitoxin; and for severe disease, 80,000 to 100,000 units of antitoxin.
Give diphtheria antitoxin at first suspicion of illness. B
Give penicillin or erythromycin to prevent transmission to contacts. A
Patients should be hospitalized with close monitoring of the cardiorespiratory function. C
While antitoxin is the first-line and most effective therapy, antibiotics should be prescribed to prevent transmission to susceptible contacts.
For the severely ill adult patient, give procaine penicillin G IM at dosage 600,000 units IM Q 12 hours until patient can swallow. Erythromycin 500 mg IV can also be used.

Once medication is taken orally, switch to oral penicillin V 125 to 250 mg qid for 14 days total. Erythromycin 500 mg PO QID for 14 days can also be used. Erythromycin is approved as a safe alternative to penicillin according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
Erythromycin is more effective in treating carriers than penicillin because of its better penetration of the infected media.

For patients who are allergic to penicillin and cannot take erythromycin, rifampin or clindamycin are alternatives. Newer macrolides (azithromycin and clarithromycin) are active in vitro but have not been studied in clinical trials.
Otolaryngic assessment is needed as part of critical care in patients with severe respiratory or neurologic compromise.
Diphtheria antitoxin must be given in all cases of suspected diphtheria; however, it is not recommended for treatment of the asymptomatic carrier.

Dose for mild disease is 20,000 to 40,000 units of antitoxin; for moderate disease is 40,000 to 60,000 units of antitoxin; and for severe disease is 80,000 to 100,000 units of antitoxin. See for dosing.
Intravenous hydrocortisone 2 to 4 mg/kg/d for 5 to 7 days has been found to be effective in patients with severe tonsillar and/or pharyngeal swelling.
Antitoxin is only available from the CDC (404-639-8257 or 770-488-7100).
Antitoxin levels should be measured after 6 months in patients who received the diphtheria antitoxin.
When diphtheria is suspected, the patient should be hospitalized in respiratory isolation.
Close monitoring of respiratory and cardiac function is mandatory in the hospitalized patient.
The patient should remain hospitalized until three negative consecutive cultures of the oropharynx have been obtained after completion of therapy.
Bronchoscopy or laryngoscopy may be needed to remove membrane and alleviate airway obstruction.
Airway obstruction continues to pose a risk of death to untreated patients. Mortality rate is as high as 10% to 15%.

Dysphagia and nasal speech are the first indication of neurological involvement. In 10% to 20% of patients, paralysis of the palate and hypopharynx can occur as early as the first 10 days. Phrenic nerve involvement can cause diaphragmatic paralysis between the first and seventh weeks of illness.

Cardiac involvement (initially indicated by tachycardia) is a common cause of diphtheria-related mortality. This can occur as early as the first 10 days or as late as week 2 or 3 of illness. Arrhythmias such as first-, second-, or third-degree heart block, including cardiomyopathies, can also occur in untreated patients.

The longer the time interval between presentation and antitoxin administration, the worse the prognosis. While mortality from diphtheria is 1% in patients who receive therapy on day 1 of illness, it rises to 20% in those whose treatment is withheld until day 4. B

The prognosis depends on virulence of the organism, immunization status, patient's age, site of infection, diphtheria toxin antibody level, and most important, the timing of antitoxin administration. C

Cardiac complications such as toxic-dilated cardiomyopathy most frequently occur in patients with severe diphtheric pharyngitis. Death from diphtheria is mostly caused by cardiac involvement or airway obstruction. C
One-third of carriers undergo spontaneous resolution without treatment. C
Caution in pregnancy is based on fetal risk indicated in some animal studies.
The CDC recommends that pregnant women not vaccinated previously with Tdap receive Tdap in the immediate postpartum period.

If there is an indication for tetanus or diphtheria protection during pregnancy (i.e., high-risk wound or exposure), there are two options: receive Td during pregnancy for tetanus and diphtheria, or defer the Td vaccine indicated during pregnancy to substitute Tdap vaccine in the immediate postpartum period if the woman is likely to have sufficient protection against tetanus and diphtheria.

Consider benzyl penicillin 50,000 units/kg/day IM in two divided doses for 5 days, then 50 mg/kg/day divided tid or qid for a total of 14 days. An alternative is erythromycin 50 mg/kg/day orally or IV divided bid or qid (total dose not to exceed 2 g/day), followed by the same dose orally in 4 divided doses per day.
For cutaneous diphtheria, treatment duration is 7 to 10 days.
If cultures are positive after two weeks, treatment may be repeated for another 10 days.

Pharyngeal or laryngeal disease of 2 days duration 20,000-40,000 units
Nasopharyngeal disease 40,000-60,000 units

Skin lesions only (for cases where treatment is indicated) 20,000-40,000 units
